references.text: In Matthew's account of the last meal, the disciples ask, "Surely not I, Lord?" – they began to ask one another which of them would betray Jesus ([ref:Matt 26:22|Matthew 26:22]).
Mark tells the same story: the disciples were sorrowful and began one by one to say to him, "Surely not I?" ([ref:Mark 14:19|Mark 14:19]).
In John's Gospel we see the same reaction: the disciples looked at one another, uncertain about whom Jesus was speaking ([ref:John 13:22|John 13:22]).

Simon Peter nods to the disciple whom Jesus loved, asking him to find out who the betrayer is – yet another sign that the disciples were discussing among themselves who it might be ([ref:John 13:25|John 13:25]).
The immediate context: Jesus has just said that the betrayer's hand is with him at the table, which triggers the discussion among the disciples ([ref:Luke 22:21|Luke 22:21]).

The discussion among the disciples in Luke 22:23 about who would do this recalls a previous dispute among them – which of them was the greatest – something that also appears shortly afterward in [ref:Luke 22:24|Luke 22:24]. Already in [ref:Luke 9:46|Luke 9:46] a similar dispute arose among the disciples.

Right after the discussion about who the betrayer is, a new conflict arises among the disciples over which of them should be considered the greatest – this shows a persistent tendency toward mutual comparison ([ref:Luke 22:24|Luke 22:24]).
